title: Bound for Jerusalem
sum: Paul and his companions sail from Miletus down the coast and across the open sea to Tyre, then on to Ptolemais and Caesarea. At every stop believers warn him. At Tyre they tell him "through the Spirit" not to go up to Jerusalem. At Caesarea, in the house of Philip the evangelist, whose four daughters prophesy, the prophet Agabus ties his own hands and feet with Paul's belt: this is what will happen to its owner. Everyone begs Paul to turn back. He answers that he is ready not only to be bound but to die for the name of the Lord Jesus.

In Jerusalem, James and the elders welcome him and praise God for the Gentiles. But tens of thousands of Jewish believers have heard that Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses. To prove the rumor false, Paul joins four men completing a vow and pays their costs in the temple. Near the end of the seven days, Jews from Asia spot him, accuse him of bringing a Greek into the inner courts, and the city erupts. The Roman commander rescues him from a beating, chains him, and on the steps of the fortress Paul asks to speak to the people.
readings: Most historians accept the core: Paul came to Jerusalem around AD 57 with Gentile companions and a collection for the poor (Romans 15:25–31), took part in a temple rite at the elders' request, and was arrested after a riot over the temple's purity. The setting checks out against Josephus and the temple warning inscriptions: the Antonia fortress with its stairs, a garrison on alert at the festivals, the Egyptian prophet and the Sicarii under Felix. Debated points: whether the rumor about Paul was true, and why Luke says nothing of the collection here.

Luke tells Paul's last journey to Jerusalem as an echo of Jesus' own: warned, determined, handed over to the Gentiles, mobbed in the temple, with the crowd crying "Away with him!" The "we" narrator brings the reader along until the moment Paul goes in to James. Luke shows the Jerusalem church as loyal to the law and Paul as willing to honor it, so the riot is the work of a few accusers acting on a false assumption.

For many Christians the chapter is about faithful courage: Paul's "not only bound, but to die there" (21:13) has been read at ordinations and in times of persecution. It also raises a hard question the fathers argued over: whether Paul could rightly keep Jewish rites after the gospel. Philip's prophesying daughters have been cited for centuries in debates about women's ministry.

views.H: The route, harbors and sailing times fit what is known of shipping in the eastern Mediterranean in early summer. Jerusalem in the late 50s was tense: Felix's harsh rule, the Sicarii's knife murders at the festivals, prophets leading crowds into the wilderness. The temple warning inscriptions, two of which survive, show why a rumor that Paul had brought a Gentile past the barrier could set off a riot, and Josephus' descriptions of the Antonia and its stairs match the scene of Paul's rescue.
views.C: The "we" passage ends at 21:18. If the author was there, the Jerusalem scenes may rest on his own memory; if not, on a source or on Luke's craft. Critics since F. C. Baur have asked whether the Paul of Acts, who sponsors temple sacrifices, is the Paul of Galatians. Others, especially in the "Paul within Judaism" school, think the two fit: Paul freed Gentiles from the law, not Jews. The silence about the collection, the purpose of the trip in Paul's own letters, is widely discussed; it is mentioned only at 24:17.
views.L: The chapter is built from three farewells and three warnings (Tyre, Caesarea, Agabus), each sharper than the last, then a sudden turn from welcome to violence in Jerusalem. Agabus' prophecy, "hand him over into the hands of the Gentiles," deliberately echoes Jesus' words in Luke 18:32. The accusation against Paul repeats the charge against Stephen (6:13), and the crowd's cry repeats the cry against Jesus. The chapter ends on a cliffhanger: a prisoner in chains raising his hand for silence.
views.J: This is one of the most important chapters in the New Testament for Jewish readers, because it shows the Jerusalem church as a law-keeping Jewish movement, "zealous for the law," and Paul willing to prove he keeps it too. Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen and Mark Nanos argue that Paul never told Jews to stop observing the law, and that this chapter preserves the truth of that. The riot itself arises not from "the Jews" in general but from Diaspora Jews from Asia who had opposed Paul there, acting on a mistaken assumption about the temple's holiness, a holiness that Rome itself respected.
views.T: The fathers asked whether Paul's vow was sincere observance or wise accommodation (1 Corinthians 9:20). Augustine and Jerome argued it out in letters (see the deep dive). Chrysostom praised Paul's readiness to die as the model of apostolic courage. Philip's daughters are honored as an example of the gift of prophecy given to women (see the card on 21:9), and the churches still differ on whether Jewish believers may keep the law, as Paul does here (see the card on 21:20–26).

deep.h: The collection Luke does not mention
deep.b:
Paul's letters say why he went to Jerusalem: to bring the money he had collected from the Gentile churches of Macedonia, Achaia and Galatia for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9). He saw the gift as a bond between Gentile and Jewish believers, and he was afraid it might not be accepted (Romans 15:31). The list of companions in 20:4, one or two from each region, looks like the delegation that carried it.

Yet Acts does not mention the collection in this chapter. Paul refers to it only once, when he tells Felix he came to bring gifts for his nation (24:17). Scholars suggest several reasons: the gift was received quietly and Luke saw no need to tell of it; it was refused, or accepted only on the condition that Paul show his loyalty to the law, and Luke passed over an awkward moment; or some of it went to pay for the four men's offerings. None of these can be proved. What is clear is that Paul's own hope, that the gift would unite the church, stands behind the elders' plan and the riot that wrecked it.

deep.h: Did Paul compromise? Augustine and Jerome
deep.b:
Paul wrote that he became like a Jew to Jews and like someone outside the law to those outside it, to win both (1 Corinthians 9:19–23). Was his temple vow sincere, or a show? Around AD 394–405 Augustine and Jerome argued this in a famous exchange of letters, starting from Peter and Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14).

  • Jerome held that after the gospel, keeping the ceremonies of the law was wrong for Christians, and that the apostles' observance was a form of strategy, not belief.
  • Augustine answered that Paul kept the rites sincerely. In the apostles' time, he said, the old ceremonies were "dead" but not yet "deadly": they no longer gave life, but they could be kept with honor by Jewish believers until they were buried with respect. To pretend, he argued, would make Scripture a lie.

Modern readers still divide along similar lines. Many Protestant interpreters read 21:26 as accommodation for the sake of peace. Scholars of the "Paul within Judaism" view take it as a plain sign that Paul remained a law-observant Jew. Messianic Jewish congregations cite this chapter for keeping the law today.

deep.title: Claude's theory: who decides what is common?
deep.b: The accusers shout that Paul "made this holy place common" (21:28). The verb is koinoō, from koinos, "common." It is the same word at the heart of Peter's vision: "What God has made clean, you must not call common" (10:15), which Peter learned to apply to people, Gentiles included (10:28). Commentators have noticed the shared word. My suggestion is that Luke uses it to frame the whole second half of Acts. In chapter 10, God teaches the church not to call Gentiles "common." In chapter 21, the charge that brings Paul to trial is that he made the temple "common" by bringing in a Gentile. The trial that follows is about this question: who decides what is common, the barrier in the temple or the God who cleansed the Gentiles' hearts by faith (15:9)? Luke, in this reading, does not have Paul break the temple's rule; the charge is false (21:29). But he lets the word ring.

echoes: Luke 9:51; Luke 18:31–33; Luke 22:42; Luke 23:18; John 19:15; Numbers 6:1–21; Isaiah 20:2–4; Jeremiah 13:1–11; Joel 2:28; Acts 6:13; Acts 10:14–15; Acts 11:27–28; Acts 15:20, 29; Romans 15:25–31; 1 Corinthians 9:19–23; Galatians 2:9

settings.by: the disciples at Tyre, speaking through the Spirit
settings.to: Paul, during his seven-day stop while the ship unloaded
settings.when: on the way to Jerusalem for Pentecost, around AD 57
settings.why: to pass on what the Spirit showed them about danger in Jerusalem, and, out of love, to urge him not to go
settings.readers: Luke's readers learn that Paul went to his arrest with open eyes, warned again and again, and that the Spirit's warnings were about suffering, not a ban on obeying his call (20:22–23).

settings.by: Agabus, a prophet from Judea
settings.to: Paul and his companions, with the believers in Philip's house at Caesarea
settings.when: during a stay of some days at Caesarea
settings.why: to show by a sign what awaits Paul in Jerusalem: binding by the Jews and handing over to the Gentiles. The sign is a prophet's warning, not an order
settings.readers: Readers who knew Jesus' words that the Son of Man would be handed over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32) saw that Paul was walking his Lord's road.

settings.what: Paul's answer to his friends' pleading
settings.by: Paul, then the whole group
settings.to: his traveling companions (the "we") and the believers of Caesarea
settings.when: after Agabus' prophecy
settings.why: to settle the question: Paul will go, ready for chains or death, and his friends give the matter over to the Lord's will
settings.readers: For churches under pressure, a picture of courage that does not deny danger and of friends who stop pleading and pray.

settings.by: James and the elders of the Jerusalem church
settings.to: Paul and his companions, in a meeting at James' house
settings.when: the day after Paul reached Jerusalem
settings.why: to answer the rumor that Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses, and to protect both Paul and the unity of the church: if Paul publicly sponsors a temple vow, the law-keeping believers will see he keeps the law. They also restate that Gentile believers are bound only by the decree of 15:29, so no new burden falls on Gentiles
settings.readers: Luke's readers, many of them Gentiles, learned that the Jewish church was law-observant with God's blessing, that Gentiles were free of circumcision, and that Paul belonged to both.
views: Paul taught Gentiles they need not keep the law but never told Jews to abandon it (Fredriksen, Nanos).
Paul's teaching that the law does not put anyone right with God loosened Jewish observance in practice, and the elders' plan was a compromise (many Protestant interpreters).

settings.by: Jews from the province of Asia
settings.to: the crowd of worshipers in the temple courts, "Israelites"
settings.when: near the end of Paul's seven days of purification, during the festival season
settings.why: to rally the crowd against Paul as an enemy of the people, the law and the temple, and to charge him with a crime the temple inscriptions said deserved death
settings.readers: Luke's readers hear the old charge against Stephen and Jesus again, and are told plainly that it rested on a mistaken assumption (21:29).

settings.by: Paul and Claudius Lysias, the commander
settings.to: each other, at the top of the stairs to the Antonia
settings.when: as the soldiers carried Paul from the mob
settings.why: Paul asks leave to speak; the commander, surprised by his Greek, had taken him for the Egyptian rebel. Paul identifies himself as a Jew and a citizen of Tarsus, a man of standing, not a bandit
settings.readers: Readers, and perhaps Roman officials among them, see that the Christian leader was no revolutionary but an educated citizen.

traditions.q: Philip's four daughters "prophesied" (21:9). Is prophesying the same as preaching or holding church office, so that their example opens the pulpit and ordination to women?
views: Prophecy is a gift of the Spirit that women have always received, and the Church honors women prophets and teachers, but it is not the same as the ordained priesthood, which the Church holds it has no authority to confer on women (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994; Catechism 1577).

The Orthodox honor Philip's daughters and other women as prophets and saints, some called "equal to the apostles," and keep the priesthood for men, a position restated by the Inter-Orthodox consultation at Rhodes in 1988, which also urged the revival of the order of deaconesses. Women served as deaconesses in parts of the church's history, and the Patriarchate of Alexandria began ordaining deaconesses again in Africa in 2017.

Many Pentecostals cite Philip's daughters, with Joel's promise that "your daughters will prophesy" (2:17), as proof that the Spirit calls women to speak for God, and the Assemblies of God ordains women to every ministry.

Southern Baptists distinguish prophesying from the pastoral office, which the Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 6) limits to men; women may teach and serve in many other ways. Other Baptist bodies ordain women.
Methodists ordain women. John Wesley allowed some women with an extraordinary call to preach, and the Methodist Church in the United States gave women full clergy rights in 1956.

Reformed churches are divided. Some treat New Testament prophecy as a gift distinct from the teaching office of elders, which they keep for men (Presbyterian Church in America); others ordain women as ministers and elders (Presbyterian Church USA, many Reformed churches in Europe).

traditions.q: James and the elders want everyone to see that Paul, too, can "walk in line with the law and keep it" (21:24), and he joins a purification and pays for temple offerings (21:26). Should Jewish believers in Jesus keep the law of Moses today?
views: Many Messianic Jewish teachers hold that Jewish believers are still called to keep the Torah as part of God's lasting covenant with Israel, and they read 21:20–26 as showing that the apostles did so and that Paul never taught Jews to give it up. Mark Kinzer argues that Torah observance is a covenant duty for Jewish disciples of Jesus, not only a heritage; others in the movement treat it as a free expression of Jewish identity. All agree it is not required of Gentile believers (21:25).

The Council of Florence taught that the ceremonies of the law of Moses ended with Christ's coming and that, once the gospel was proclaimed, they could not be kept as necessary for salvation without sin (Cantate Domino, 1442). Following Augustine, Thomas Aquinas held that in the apostles' time the ceremonies were "dead" but not yet "deadly," which explains Paul's vow. Modern Catholic teaching also speaks with deep respect of the Jewish people and their covenant (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 839), and some Catholic theologians now leave room for Jewish Catholics to keep Jewish customs.

The fathers read Paul's vow as a wise accommodation for the sake of weaker believers. John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter, says Paul kept the custom to win the Jewish believers, not because the law was still needed. The Orthodox Church teaches that the ceremonial law was fulfilled in Christ and is not binding on any Christian, Jewish or Gentile.

The Augsburg Confession teaches that the ceremonies of the law of Moses are not necessary for salvation, and that to require them as necessary obscures the gospel (article 28). Such customs are "adiaphora," things neither commanded nor forbidden, which a Christian may freely keep out of love but never as a condition of righteousness (Formula of Concord, article 10). Lutherans read Paul's vow in that light: freedom used for the sake of others.

The Westminster Confession teaches that the ceremonial laws, given to Israel as types of Christ, "are now abrogated under the New Testament" (19.3), while the moral law still binds everyone. Calvin, commenting on this chapter, defended Paul's vow as an indifferent act done for a time, out of love for weak Jewish believers, while the ceremonies were being laid aside.

Classic dispensationalists teach that the law of Moses, given to Israel, ended as a rule of life at the cross, for Jewish and Gentile believers alike, and that the church lives under grace (the Scofield Reference Bible; Charles Ryrie). Many read Paul's vow as an act from the book's transitional period, not a pattern for the church today.

title: The Speech from the Stairs
sum: Standing on the steps of the fortress, in chains, Paul speaks to the crowd that had just tried to kill him. He speaks in Hebrew, and they fall silent. He tells them who he is: a Jew raised in Jerusalem, trained by Gamaliel, as zealous for God as they are, a former persecutor of "the Way." Then he tells how, on the road to Damascus at noon, a light from heaven knocked him down and Jesus the Nazarene spoke to him; how Ananias, a devout and law-keeping Jew, restored his sight and told him to be baptized; and how later, praying in this same temple, he saw the Lord, who sent him away to the Gentiles.

At the word "Gentiles" the crowd erupts again. The commander orders Paul flogged to get the truth out of him. As they tie him down, Paul asks the centurion whether it is legal to whip a Roman citizen who has not been tried. The interrogation stops at once. The commander, who bought his own citizenship, learns that Paul was born a citizen. The next day, still wanting to know the charge, he calls the chief priests and the Sanhedrin together and brings Paul before them.
readings: Paul's speech follows the pattern of a courtroom defense: an opening that wins goodwill (he speaks Hebrew, calls them "brothers and fathers," praises their zeal), a narrative of the facts, and an appeal to witnesses: the high priest, the elders, Ananias, the Lord himself. Each part answers the charge of 21:28 that he is against the people, the law and the temple. It stops where the crowd stopped it, at the word "Gentiles."
Read as the second telling of Paul's call

This is the second of three accounts of the Damascus road (9; 22; 26). Read side by side, they differ in details (who heard the voice, Ananias' role, where Paul's commission came from), and each fits its hearers: here, a Jewish crowd hears of a law-keeping Ananias and a vision in their temple. Readers have taken the differences as signs of Luke's art, his sources, or ordinary retelling.

Christians have long read the speech as the model of personal testimony: who I was, what happened when I met Jesus, and what he sent me to do. Its center, "have your sins washed away as you call on his name" (22:16), is also one of the key verses in the churches' debates about baptism.

views.H: Roman law protected citizens from flogging without trial (Cicero's speech against Verres shows how seriously); Paul invoked it at the last moment. Citizenship could be bought under Claudius, as Cassius Dio reports, which fits a tribune named Claudius Lysias. Interrogation by scourging was routine for non-citizens. The use of Aramaic or Hebrew in a Jerusalem crowd and Greek with a Roman officer reflects the city's languages. Whether a tribune could convene the Sanhedrin is debated; Sherwin-White found it plausible as an informal hearing.
views.C: The speech is a showcase of Luke's method with speeches, which ancient historians composed to fit the speaker and occasion (Thucydides 1.22). The shaping is plain: Ananias becomes a pious Jew, the commission comes in the temple, Jesus is "the Righteous One." Critical scholars stress the differences from chapters 9 and 26; others note that Paul's own letters confirm the core (Galatians 1:13–17; 1 Corinthians 15:8–9). Some historians doubt Paul held Roman citizenship, since his letters never mention it and he received synagogue and Roman beatings (2 Corinthians 11:24–25); most accept Luke's report.
views.L: The speech answers the three charges of 21:28 point by point and is cut off at its climax, as Stephen's was (7:54–57). The crowd's "Take such a man off the face of the earth!" repeats the cry of 21:36. Then the story turns from the mob to Roman law: one sentence from Paul stops the whip. The chapter ends by setting up the hearing before the Sanhedrin, the next station in a sequence of trials that parallels Jesus' passion.
views.J: Paul presents himself as a loyal Jew who never left Judaism: born a Jew, raised in Jerusalem, a student of the great Pharisee Gamaliel, called by "the God of our ancestors" through a respected, law-keeping Jew. Jewish scholars such as Alan Segal have read Paul's experience as a real conversion within Judaism, from one Jewish group to another, and compared it with Jewish mystical visions. The crowd's anger at the mention of the Gentiles reflects the explosive charge of 21:28, not a Jewish refusal to share God with the nations; Judaism welcomed converts and God-fearers.
views.T: Chrysostom praised Paul's wisdom in speaking Hebrew and in naming Gamaliel and Ananias as witnesses. In sacramental traditions, 22:16 is a classic text for baptism as the washing away of sin (Catechism 1263; the Nicene Creed's "one baptism for the forgiveness of sins"). Paul's appeal to his citizenship has been cited in Christian ethics as proof that believers may use legal rights to protect themselves.

deep.b:
Acts tells the Damascus road three times: in Luke's own narration (9:1–19), in this speech to a Jewish crowd (22:3–16), and in Paul's speech to King Agrippa (26:9–18). The words of Jesus' question are the same each time: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" The rest varies:

  • The companions. In 9:7 they hear the voice but see no one; in 22:9 they see the light but do not hear the voice; in 26:14 they all fall to the ground.
  • The time. Only 22:6 and 26:13 say it was midday.
  • Ananias. In 9:10–17 he is a disciple who receives a vision; in 22:12–16 he is a devout Jew respected by all the Jews of Damascus; in 26 he is not mentioned.
  • The commission. In 9:15 the Lord tells Ananias Paul's mission; in 22:14–15 Ananias tells Paul, and the sending to the Gentiles comes later in the temple (22:21); in 26:16–18 Jesus gives it directly on the road, in words that recall the calls of Jeremiah and the servant of Isaiah.
  • The goads. Only 26:14 has "It is hard for you to kick against the goads."

Three explanations are offered, often in combination. Luke shaped each telling for its hearers, as ancient historians did. Luke used different sources. Or the differences are the natural variations of a story told many times. Luke repeats Peter's vision too (10; 11), and repetition in ancient narrative marks importance. Paul's own letters speak of the event more briefly: he says he has seen Jesus the Lord (1 Corinthians 9:1), and that God revealed his Son in him so that he might preach him among the Gentiles (Galatians 1:15–16).

Only Acts says so (16:37–38; 22:25–29; 23:27; 25:10–12). Paul's letters never mention it, and he says he was beaten with rods three times (2 Corinthians 11:25), the punishment a citizen was supposed to be spared. A few scholars therefore think Luke invented the citizenship to explain Paul's appeal to Caesar and his journey to Rome.

Most historians accept it. Paul's letters had no reason to mention it; the laws protecting citizens were often broken by local officials, as Cicero's speech against Verres shows; and Paul's appeal to Caesar and transfer to Rome make little sense for a non-citizen. His name Paul (Paulus) is a Roman name (a cognomen, the last of a citizen's three names). How his family gained citizenship is unknown, though freed slaves of Roman citizens became citizens, and Jerome's report that his family came from Gischala in Galilee as prisoners of war would fit that path.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the speech answers the charges in order
deep.b: The accusation in 21:28 has three parts: Paul teaches "against the people, against the law and against this place." Commentators note that the speech answers the charges in general. I suggest it answers them in that order. Against the people: Paul opens by claiming the people as his own: a Jew, raised in this city, zealous for God "the same as every one of you" (22:3–5). Against the law: the man who brought him to faith was "devout, as the law measures it," respected by all the Jews (22:12), and spoke of "the God of our ancestors" (22:14). Against this place: his mission came to him while praying "in the temple" (22:17). The speech breaks off exactly where it reaches the fourth matter, the Gentiles (22:21), which was the real cause of the riot (21:28–29). If this reading is right, the speech is complete as a defense; what the crowd refused to hear was the one thing Paul would not leave out.

echoes: Acts 7:2, 54–58; Acts 8:1–3; Acts 9:1–30; Acts 16:37–38; Acts 26:9–18; Isaiah 6:1–9; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 53:11; Joel 2:32; Galatians 1:13–17; Philippians 3:4–6; 1 Corinthians 15:8–9; 2 Corinthians 11:24–25; Luke 21:12–15

settings.by: Paul, in chains, speaking Hebrew (or Aramaic)
settings.to: the Jewish crowd in the temple's outer court below the Antonia stairs, many of them pilgrims, who had just tried to kill him; Roman soldiers listening
settings.when: moments after his rescue from the mob, with the commander's permission
settings.why: to answer the charge that he was against the people, the law and the temple (21:28) by telling his own story: a zealous Jew whom the God of Israel turned around and sent, through a vision in this very temple, to the Gentiles. He seeks to be heard as a fellow Jew, not to win an argument
settings.readers: Luke's readers hear the second account of Paul's call, shaped for Jewish hearers, and see that the mission to the Gentiles came from Israel's God in Israel's temple, not from Paul's rejection of his people.

settings.what: The words of Jesus on the road
settings.by: Jesus, the voice from heaven
settings.to: Saul, fallen on the road near Damascus; his companions saw the light but did not hear the words
settings.when: at midday, as Saul neared Damascus to arrest believers
settings.why: to stop the persecutor, reveal who he was really persecuting, and send him into the city to learn his task
settings.readers: Readers hear the same question in all three accounts, and learn that to persecute the church is to persecute its Lord.

settings.by: Ananias, a devout Jew of Damascus
settings.to: Saul, blind in Damascus
settings.when: three days after the vision on the road (9:9)
settings.why: to tell Saul that the God of their ancestors chose him to see the Righteous One and be his witness to everyone, and to call him to be baptized and have his sins washed away
settings.readers: For the crowd, a respected Jew vouches for Paul. For Luke's readers, the words join faith, baptism and forgiveness, a link the churches have read in different ways.

settings.what: The Lord's word in the temple
settings.by: the Lord Jesus, in a vision
settings.to: Paul, praying in the temple during a visit to Jerusalem after his conversion
settings.when: probably his first visit, about three years after Damascus (Galatians 1:18)
settings.why: to send Paul away from Jerusalem, where his witness would not be received, and out to the Gentiles far away
settings.readers: Readers learn that Paul's Gentile mission was not his own idea or a slight to Jerusalem, but a command received in the temple itself.

settings.by: the crowd in the temple court
settings.to: the commander and soldiers, and to Paul
settings.when: the moment Paul said "the Gentiles"
settings.why: to demand Paul's death, as one who should never have been allowed to live
settings.readers: The cry repeats 21:36 and the cry against Jesus, and Luke's readers see another unfinished speech, like Stephen's.

settings.by: Paul, then the centurion and the commander
settings.to: the centurion supervising the flogging, and then the commander
settings.when: inside the barracks, as Paul was tied for interrogation by the whip
settings.why: to stop an illegal flogging by claiming the protection Roman law gave citizens, and so to change how Rome would treat him from then on
settings.readers: Luke's readers, some of whom faced Roman courts, see that a Christian could rightly use the law's protection, and that Paul was a man of standing in Roman terms.

traditions.q: Ananias told Saul, "have yourself baptized, and have your sins washed away as you call on his name" (22:16). Are sins actually washed away in baptism, or is baptism the sign of a washing received by faith?
views: Baptism truly washes away all sins, original and personal, and gives new life; the Catechism (1263) teaches that by baptism all sins are forgiven. Faith is required in adults, and baptism is its sacrament.
Baptism is the washing of rebirth in which the person dies and rises with Christ and is cleansed from sin, as the Creed says: "one baptism for the remission of sins."
Baptism "works forgiveness of sins" because God's word is joined to the water, and faith receives what the word promises (Small Catechism, on baptism).

Baptism is a sign and seal of the washing away of sin by Christ's blood and Spirit; the grace it signifies is given to those who believe, though not tied to the moment of baptism (Westminster Confession 28.1, 28.6).

Baptism is a believer's act of obedience that pictures the washing already received by faith; Paul had already met the risen Lord and "called on his name." Baptism does not itself remove sin (Baptist Faith and Message, article 7).
Churches of Christ read 22:16 with 2:38 as showing that sins are forgiven when a believer is baptized: Saul believed on the road but was told to be baptized to wash his sins away.

title: Hope on Trial
sum: Before the Sanhedrin, Paul declares that he has lived before God with a good conscience. The high priest Ananias has him struck on the mouth, and Paul flares back: "God will be the one to strike you, you wall painted with whitewash!" Told whom he has insulted, he apologizes and quotes the law. Then, seeing that the council is divided between Sadducees and Pharisees, he cries out that he is a Pharisee on trial for the hope of the resurrection. The council splits; some Pharisee scribes take his side, and the commander has to pull Paul out before he is torn apart. That night the Lord stands by him: as he has testified in Jerusalem, he must testify in Rome.

The next morning more than forty men swear an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul, and ask the chief priests to lure him out for another hearing. Paul's nephew hears of the ambush and tells Paul, then the commander. That night the commander sends Paul to Caesarea with 470 soldiers and a letter to the governor, Felix, saying he has found no charge deserving death or chains. Felix agrees to hear the case when the accusers arrive and keeps Paul under guard in Herod's palace.
readings: The cast is historical: Ananias son of Nedebaeus, a greedy and violent high priest later murdered by rebels; Felix, the freedman governor whom Tacitus despised; a Roman tribune with a purchased citizenship. The division between Pharisees and Sadducees over the resurrection is confirmed by Josephus and the Gospels. The plot fits the violent years before the revolt. Historians debate the size of the escort, the overnight march to Antipatris, and how Luke knew the letter's wording.
Read as Luke's parallel to the passion

Paul is struck before the high priest, as Jesus was; judged before the Sanhedrin and then a Roman governor; declared innocent by Pharisee scribes and by a Roman officer, as Pilate declared Jesus innocent three times. Unlike Jesus, Paul is rescued, and the Lord's "you must bear witness in Rome" turns the story toward its goal.
Read as a word of courage

Christians have long drawn comfort from 23:11: in the worst night of Paul's life, after a riot, a flogging stopped at the last moment and a near lynching in the council, the Lord stood by him and said "Be brave." The quiet help of an unnamed nephew and an alert officer shows God's care working through ordinary people.

views.H: Ananias' record in Josephus (greed, violence, assassination in 66) fits Paul's outburst and its later reading as prophecy. The Antonia garrison, the road down to Antipatris and on to Caesarea, and Herod's seaside palace there are well known. A Roman officer's letter to his governor, his care to protect a citizen and himself, and Felix's question about Paul's home province all fit Roman practice as described by Sherwin-White.
views.C: Critical scholars ask how Paul, raised in Jerusalem, could fail to recognize the high priest; how a whole council could split over one sentence; and whether an escort of 470 for one prisoner is believable. Some see Luke's hand in the neat pattern of Roman fairness and Jewish hostility. Others note how many details Luke gets right and how little he flatters anyone, including Paul. The Western text adds a motive for the large escort (see the variant at 23:24).
views.L: The chapter has three scenes of danger (the council, the plot, the night ride) each followed by rescue, with the Lord's word at the center (23:11). Luke enjoys irony: Paul insults the high priest without knowing it; the forty swear not to eat; the commander's letter rewrites his own role. The nephew is the only member of Paul's family ever mentioned in a story, and he appears just long enough to save Paul's life.
views.J: Paul's claim "I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees" is in the present tense: he still counts himself one, and the Pharisee scribes defend him. Jewish scholars note that the Pharisees in Acts are often friendly (Gamaliel in 5:34–39, believers in 15:5, the scribes here), and that the hostile group is the priestly leadership. The resurrection hope that divides the council was a central Pharisaic belief that later became part of rabbinic Judaism (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). The plot of the forty should not be blamed on the Jewish people; it was a sworn band in a violent time.
views.T: Paul's apology in 23:5, quoting Exodus 22:28, has been used in Christian teaching on respect for church and civil authorities even when they are unworthy. Augustine read the "whitewashed wall" as prophecy, not anger. The Lord's words in 23:11 have been read in many traditions as a promise of God's presence to those who suffer for the faith. Chrysostom's homilies dwell on God's care in the nephew's timely news.

deep.b:
Luke tells Paul's trials (chapters 21–26) with many echoes of Jesus' passion in his Gospel:

  • a journey to Jerusalem undertaken knowing what waits there (Luke 9:51; Acts 20:22–24; 21:13);
  • a prophecy of being handed over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32; Acts 21:11);
  • a crowd shouting for him to be taken away (Luke 23:18; Acts 21:36; 22:22);
  • a slap or blow at a hearing before the high priest (John 18:22; Acts 23:2);
  • hearings before the Sanhedrin, a Roman governor and a Herod (Luke 22:66–23:12; Acts 23:1; 24; 25–26);
  • repeated declarations of innocence by officials (Luke 23:4, 14, 22; Acts 23:9, 29; 25:25; 26:31–32).

The parallels are widely noted (Talbert, Tannehill, Pervo). Readers draw different conclusions. Many see Luke presenting the disciple following his master (Luke 6:40). Some critical scholars think Luke shaped events to fit the pattern. Others caution that the differences are just as striking: Paul is never crucified in Acts, the Romans protect him, and the book ends with him preaching freely.

The Sanhedrin of Paul's day included two main parties. The Sadducees were linked with the priestly aristocracy and the high priest's family. Josephus says they rejected traditions not written in the law of Moses and denied that the soul survives death or that there are rewards and punishments after it (Antiquities 18.16; Jewish War 2.164–165). The Pharisees were a lay movement of experts in the law who kept the traditions of the elders. Josephus says they believed that souls survive death and receive reward or punishment (Antiquities 18.12–14; Jewish War 2.163); Acts 23:8 adds that they affirmed the resurrection, angels and spirits.

The Gospels show the same divide (Matthew 22:23–33). After the temple was destroyed in AD 70, the Sadducees disappeared, and the Pharisees' heirs, the rabbis, shaped later Judaism. The Mishnah (about AD 200) says that one who denies the resurrection of the dead has no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). Paul's cry in 23:6 placed his faith in Jesus on the Pharisees' side of the oldest debate in the council.

In these chapters Rome looks good: the commander rescues Paul three times, honors his citizenship, protects him from assassins, and writes that he has done nothing deserving death. Many scholars have concluded that one aim of Acts was apologetic: to show Roman readers that Christianity was harmless and law-abiding, a dispute within Judaism (23:29). Others have argued the reverse. Richard Cassidy, for example, held that Luke was no friend of Rome: its officials take bribes (24:26), play politics (24:27; 25:9) and keep an innocent man in chains for years. A third view is that Luke wrote mainly for Christians, to assure them that their faith and their apostle were innocent in the eyes of the law even though Paul died a Roman prisoner. The chapter supports all three in part, which may be the point: Rome is neither hero nor villain, but the means by which God gets Paul to Rome (23:11).

echoes: Exodus 22:28; Leviticus 19:15; Ezekiel 13:10–16; Matthew 22:23–33; Matthew 23:27; John 18:22–23; Luke 23:4, 14, 22; Acts 4:1–2; Acts 5:34–39; Acts 15:5; Acts 18:9–10; Acts 19:21; Acts 27:23–24; Philippians 3:5; 2 Timothy 4:17

settings.by: Paul, with the high priest Ananias and his attendants
settings.to: the Sanhedrin, Pharisees and Sadducees, called together by the Roman commander, who was present to learn the charge
settings.when: the day after the riot, about AD 57
settings.why: Paul means to defend his life as faithful to God; struck unjustly, he protests, then apologizes from the law, then names the true issue, the resurrection hope, which wins the Pharisees' support and exposes the council's division
settings.readers: Luke's readers see Paul as a Pharisee still, standing for Israel's hope, and see the leaders who opposed him as divided and unjust.
views: Paul shrewdly split the council to escape (some ancient and modern readers).
Paul named what his faith rested on, Jesus' resurrection as the start of the general resurrection, as he does in every later defense (24:15; 26:6–8; 28:20).

settings.what: The Pharisee scribes' defense of Paul
settings.by: some scribes of the Pharisees' party
settings.to: the rest of the Sanhedrin, in the uproar
settings.when: after Paul's claim to be on trial for the resurrection
settings.why: to declare Paul innocent and to leave open that a spirit or angel had really spoken to him
settings.readers: One more verdict of innocence, from Jewish leaders this time, like Gamaliel's caution in 5:34–39.

settings.by: the Lord Jesus
settings.to: Paul, alone in the barracks
settings.when: the night after the hearing
settings.why: to encourage Paul after three escapes from death in two days, and to promise that he will reach Rome as a witness
settings.readers: The verse sets the course of the rest of Acts. Christians reading it in prison or persecution found in it the promise of the Lord's presence.

settings.what: The oath and plan of the forty
settings.by: more than forty conspirators
settings.to: the chief priests and the elders
settings.when: the morning after the hearing
settings.why: to bind themselves by a curse to kill Paul and to enlist the leaders in luring him out of the fortress for a staged hearing
settings.readers: Luke shows how far the hostility had gone, and how God's promise of 23:11 would be kept against it.

settings.by: the son of Paul's sister
settings.to: Paul, then the commander, in private
settings.when: the same day
settings.why: to expose the ambush in time; the commander swears him to secrecy so the plotters will not know they are found out
settings.readers: Readers see God's care working through a relative and a careful officer.

settings.by: Claudius Lysias
settings.to: two centurions
settings.when: that evening, for departure at about nine at night
settings.why: to move Paul out of Jerusalem under a guard too large to attack and deliver him safely to the governor
settings.readers: Roman power, so often the persecutor, here protects the apostle.

settings.by: Claudius Lysias, commander in Jerusalem
settings.to: Felix, governor of Judea, at Caesarea
settings.when: sent with Paul that night
settings.why: to transfer the case, state the facts in a way that protects the writer (he rescued a Roman citizen, found no capital charge, foiled a plot), and order the accusers to Caesarea
settings.readers: Luke's readers get a Roman official's written verdict of Paul's innocence, and enjoy the self-serving edits that the story has already exposed.

settings.by: Felix, the governor
settings.to: Paul, on arrival at Caesarea
settings.when: the day after the night march
settings.why: to learn Paul's home province (to decide whether to keep the case) and to promise a full hearing when the accusers come
settings.readers: The scene sets up the trial before Felix in chapter 24.
